presentations.pitch: Flight Deck Cockpit makes every practice call a flight with one shared visual grammar. Before the call there is a pre-flight briefing: status lamps for mic level, persona loaded and goal read, and Start flight stays locked until mic and goal are green. During the call there is a dark HUD. Six rubric tape gauges move after every rep turn with their weights and tallies, such as Discovery 3 of 10. At most two coach cue cards sit on the right, each with a one-tap Use line. A mono timer and an On course lamp sit in the top bar. After the call there is a black-box debrief. It has a scrubbable timeline with a score curve and event markers, and the gauges rewind as you scrub. Evidence chips seek to the exact second a quote was said. Dark is the default only for flight and debrief. Library, wizard, logbook and team run in a daylight theme, and both themes come from one token file. The library is faceted, the wizard is five steps with confidence chips and a mandatory test flight, and there is a manager 'flight ops' view. The stack is shadcn/ui, Tailwind v4, Motion, Recharts, and Sora, Inter and JetBrains Mono. Against today's chat-bubble live screen, with its orb and a red End button beside the input, this is a different product. The visual identity is the most ownable of my five.
presentations.strongest: Craft and system coherence. Gauges, lamps and mono telemetry are one instrument vocabulary that carries from pre-flight to HUD to debrief to logbook dials. The shape rules are disciplined: hairlines instead of shadows, a 1px inner highlight, and only the live element gets a cyan glow. The type stack is specific, with tabular-nums mono so scores never jitter. The black-box replay, where the gauges rewind as you scrub, is the signature interaction. It makes the debrief the opposite of today's one long scroll. The amber Estimate lamp turns today's silent keyword-fallback F grade into an honest labelled state. The mobile long-press End and grade with a progress ring fixes the exact thumb-zone flaw visible in the current mobile-04 screenshot.
presentations.weakest: Three things. (1) The theme split is a seam. Library and wizard are daylight, then pre-flight and flight are dark. The proposal never says what theme the pre-flight screen uses. If it is daylight, the rep gets a lighting jolt exactly when they should be focusing. The proposal says light is the browsing default and dark is for live and debrief, which is a deliberate choice but a risky one. (2) The metaphor is heavy. Fly, Brief, Black box, Logbook and Flight ops will read as costume to some enterprise buyers, and six gauges plus a cue stack plus a flight-log transcript is a crowded screen for someone mid-sentence. The jurors flagged this. (3) The library is unsized. 'A large open persona set' has no count, and the facet examples omit auto, real estate, retail and recruiting. I also could not verify the stack claims. I tried the Firecrawl lookup for shadcn defaulting to Base UI and Radix status, but it was rate limited, so the 'Base UI became default in July 2026' claim is unconfirmed. The proposal itself flags that its sources disagree on Radix. XL scope, including a Tailwind 3 to 4 migration touching every screen.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Above baseline, by a modest margin. A separate grader sidecar runs after each rep turn and returns rubric deltas plus at most one cue, rendered only to the rep, so the persona stays forbidden to coach. Cues come from fixed categories with evidence quotes, and live gauges and the final grade share one rubric, so they cannot silently disagree. Honest fallback via the Estimate lamp. Gaps: no cue-latency target is stated at all, and a one-cue-per-20-seconds throttle can silence a fast call or let a cue land after its moment. It is a per-turn call, not streaming. On screen, the combination of gauges, cues and talk-track ticks is the richest live feedback surface of the five, and it is the one at most risk of overloading the rep.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: About at baseline, slightly above on UX and below on content. The wizard is strong: five steps (Source, Persona, Scenario, Rubric, Test flight), source tabs, streaming fields with confidence chips, rubric weight sliders that total 100, and a save gate behind a test flight. The same zod schema validates wizard output, CI and contributor PRs. Facets cover role, industry, difficulty, objection type and mode, with counts and 'flown N times' social proof. But the seed library is never sized or dated, so a brief that asks for every sales job at open-source level has no number to check against. UI is good, content commitment is vague.

presentations.pitch: Call Canvas is a dark, spatial studio built on a dot-grid canvas. Personas, talk-track steps and rubric criteria are nodes you can wire together. The library has a card grid by default and an opt-in board mode, where picked personas become React Flow nodes sequenced from warm-up to hard close. The AI wizard is a visible graph. Source nodes (job description, product URL, CRM note, pasted call, ICP) wire into a Persona Synth node. It emits Persona, Scenario and Rubric nodes, each field cites the source sentence it came from, and manual edits survive regeneration. Live call and debrief deliberately drop the canvas for fixed panels. The live call has a talk-track rail, timecoded transcript, six live rubric bars with evidence pins, a violet whisper card and an amber objection alert. The debrief has a score dial, a replay timeline with cue markers, and a view of whether the rep followed each cue. The stack is shadcn on Radix, Tailwind v4, React Flow, motion, cmdk and vaul, in Geist and Geist Mono. It has full light-mode parity, a 64px icon rail and a mobile bottom bar.
presentations.strongest: Colour semantics and the cue-followed signal. Violet is reserved for coach whispers only, and teal is for signal and status, so a rep can tell advice from status at a glance. That is a rare, real piece of system discipline. Cue markers on the debrief timeline that show whether the rep followed the advice answer the question 'did live coaching change behaviour?', which none of the other four design-answers. The wizard's per-field provenance (which source sentence produced which field) is a trust feature that also teaches users how the AI reads their input. Tokens are fully specified for both modes, and the 'OpenAI engine as a plain text chip, never a logo' choice shows brand restraint.
presentations.weakest: The headline idea does not touch the core. The proposal admits the canvas can read as a diagram tool, and it retreats to fixed panels for the live call and debrief, which are the screens that matter most. So the distinctive metaphor lives in the library board and the wizard, where it is least needed. A node-graph wizard is harder than a stepper for a sales manager who just wants to paste a job description. It also needs keyboard wiring, screen-reader labels and a touch fallback, and on a 390px phone it does not work sensibly. The dot-grid-and-nodes look is now the common visual language of n8n, Langflow and Make, so it signals AI tooling but not necessarily sales coaching. React Flow adds bundle weight and a graph model that contributors must learn just to add a pack. Launch library is 40 reviewed packs against a 140 target. Phase estimates (about two weeks each) are optimistic for XL.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Clearly above baseline on design, and the best-specified cue taxonomy in my set. Five cue types: whisper (next question), objection alert with an acknowledge-then-anchor line, talk-track progress, pace (talk ratio), and rubric delta with an evidence pin. There is a Silent, Whisper or Active coach level, Why and helpful-or-not buttons that feed prompt tuning, and an explicit latency target (2 seconds in text, 3 in voice). Live numbers are honestly labelled 'live estimate'. The persona never sees coaching. The risk is the same as everywhere: the target is unproven, and the proposal itself says that if cue latency misses, coaching falls back to post-call and D drops below baseline.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Slightly above baseline on commitment. This is the most concrete plan in my set: about 140 packs, roughly seven per industry across 20 industries, three difficulty levels each, tagged objection types, versioned JSON validated by zod and CI. It also says plainly to ship 40 reviewed packs before claiming 140. Facets cover role, industry, difficulty and objection. The wizard produces schema-validated structured output with provenance. The weakness is the creation UX: a graph is a poor fit for a first-time persona builder, and real estate is missing from the named industries. Content is honest, and the wizard interaction is the risky part.

presentations.pitch: Live Coach Studio turns the trainer into a call cockpit on one shadcn/ui system, with Tremor-style analytics blocks restyled on the same tokens and confined to the screens where analytics belong. The live call is three lanes. The transcript sits on the left and puts a criterion dot on each rep line once evidence is found. The centre has one amber coach cue at a time, with the trigger quote printed beneath it and a six-segment talk-track bar. The right lane is a live rubric where each criterion starts hatched as provisional and turns solid only when a transcript quote confirms it. The debrief has a Geist Mono score, a delta against the previous attempt, a clickable timeline strip with one tick per turn coloured by criterion, and a two-column scorecard where every number links to its transcript line. The manager view has a rep-by-criterion matrix and a calibration chart that sets AI score against manager score. Light is the default, and the live call defaults to dark. Existing routes stay, Tailwind 3.4 stays in the first phase, and a collapsible sidebar plus Cmd+K replace the glass header. The persona library is YAML validated by zod, with 15 sales jobs and a 120-persona target.
presentations.strongest: Evidence-first interaction design. The hatched-to-solid rubric fill is the best small craft idea across all five proposals. It shows 'this is an estimate' and 'this is confirmed by a quote' in the same bar without a label, and it makes live and final scores comparable line by line. The calibration chart (AI score vs manager score) is what makes a sales manager trust the grader, and no other proposal has it. Charts are kept off the live call, so the hardest screen stays calm. It is also the most buildable plan: it keeps every route, defers the Tailwind 4 move as its own change, reuses the zod schema already in the repo, and has a token-first Phase 0 of about a week. The 15 sales-job tabs match the brief's list almost word for word.
presentations.weakest: The look. shadcn is the most common component kit in React, Tremor blocks are the most common dashboard kit, and the proposal admits the app can drift into 'another default template'. That is the brief's own diagnosis of today's app. The palette (cool-grey canvas, white cards, a blue #2B50E0 primary) is close to today's blue-on-slate, and Tailwind 3.4 stays, so the styling engine is not modernised. Beyond the amber cue lane and the violet provenance chip there is no signature motion or visual language. The analytics-first push toward debrief, progress and team risks making a practice room feel like a BI tool. Two chart idioms (shadcn charts and Tremor blocks) still have to be kept consistent. A reviewer who wants a cutting-edge first impression will not get one from the screenshots alone. Only 40 of 120 launch personas are reviewed.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Above baseline and the most trustworthy design. A coach model reads the last six turns after each finalised turn and returns structured output: next best question, objection type with its trigger quote, talk-track step, and rubric deltas, each marked provisional or confirmed with an evidence line. Cues appear in under 2 seconds. Silent, Light and Full modes. 'Coach paused' is shown if the coach times out, and the call continues. The persona never hears the coach (visual only in v1). Live scoring uses the same grader prompt as the debrief. The deduction is that scoring has not been checked against human raters, which the proposal says itself, and that the 2-second target is looser than some rivals.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Slightly above baseline. It names 15 sales jobs that match the brief, five facets (job, industry, difficulty, call type, objection type) with a live result count, and a 120-persona target with a Draft badge on the unreviewed 80, which is an honest signal of depth. YAML files validated by the same zod schema the wizard uses mean a contributor's file and an AI draft have an identical shape. The wizard is four steps (Source, Draft, Shape, Dry run) with every field traced to its source sentence, and it proposes a rubric from MEDDPICC, BANT or Challenger. The weak point is review load: 80 of 120 personas ship as drafts, and a stereotyping checklist for insurance, mortgage and auto is promised but not resourced.

presentations.pitch: Broadcast Desk treats every practice call as a live stream. On the live screen the persona is a ring on a dark stage that pulses with audio levels, live captions run as a lower third, and a segment bar tracks the talk track. A 360px right rail is a coach chat: typed cue cards for nudges, objection alerts, next questions and praise, each with a glyph, a 'why' link to the transcript quote, and pin and dismiss. A left strip shows five provisional rubric bars with green or rose delta chips. After the call the debrief is replay-first. A timeline carries coach markers and three auto-marked clips such as Best moment and Missed fee question, each exportable as a 1200x630 shareable moment card. Library, wizard, pre-call, dashboard and team stay on a calm light surface. Persona cards have a 10-second 'Hear them' voice sample, the wizard requires a 60-second test drive, and the manager view has 'Import a real call' to turn a real transcript into a practice persona. The stack is Tailwind v4, shadcn on Base UI, React Aria for hard widgets, Motion and Recharts.
presentations.strongest: Two ideas the others lack. First, 'Hear them' on every persona card. A rep judges a persona by how it sounds before choosing it, which is the right interaction for a voice product and a memorable library moment. Second, the debrief-to-share loop: auto-marked highlight moments and an exportable moment card give the project a natural launch artifact and a team-sharing habit. 'Import a real call' closes the loop competitors pitch (real call to practice persona). Icon pairing, with a glyph plus colour per cue type so colour is never the only signal, is good accessibility craft. The light-by-default browse screens with a stream metaphor confined to live and replay show good restraint.
presentations.weakest: The metaphor works against the audience. 'Stage', 'clips', 'on-air red' and a coach feed that scrolls like chat can read as gamey to the sales leaders who buy this, and the proposal says so and then leans in. The coach rail is still a chat-style list, which is exactly the pattern the brief diagnoses as the problem with today's live screen, only on the side. The palette is internally inconsistent: it carries cue-blue, coach-violet, go-green, amber, alert-rose and a separate on-air red (#F25F5C), which sits almost on top of the rose (#FB7185). The proposal's reason for the split is sound, but in practice two near-identical reds will be misread. It names a 1.5-second cue target next to its own admitted 1 to 2 second coach latency. 150 generated voice samples carry TTS cost and licensing questions that are never priced. Shareable clips of calls raise a recording-consent issue the proposal names for redaction but not consent.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Slightly above baseline. Out-of-band coach, typed cues with evidence links, a pin action, and sensible rules (at most one cue per two turns, none while the persona is speaking in voice mode). The scoreboard is five provisional criterion bars with delta chips. Whispers are visual first and earbud TTS later. The deductions: the 1.5-second target is contradicted by the proposal's own latency risk, a cue every two turns is sparse, and the chat-feed form makes the coaching feel like another conversation to read while the rep is already in one. Strong on the debrief side (auto-clips), middling on the live side.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Slightly above baseline. It sets a 150-plus persona target across 20-plus sales jobs, three difficulty levels per persona, tagged objections, named collections such as 'Insurance renewals', a 'Good first persona' contributor tag, and a facet rail. The wizard takes all five source types, shows provenance chips, proposes rubric weights and a talk track, and requires a 60-second test drive. 'Hear them' and 'Import a real call' are real differentiators. The deduction is that 30 seed personas at Phase 2 against a 150 target is a big gap, and every persona needs a voice sample.

presentations.pitch: Cockpit Dark Command Center is a Linear-style, keyboard-first control room built on shadcn/ui over Radix. Dark is the default and light is a full parallel token set. Cmd-K runs everything (start a practice call by persona name, create a persona, filter the library, mute, end and grade, toggle the theme), with a visible keycap beside each command. Density is split by job. Library, progress and team are dense tables with keyboard row navigation and heatmaps. The live call is deliberately sparse: a three-pane resizable layout with a talk-track rail, a two-lane transcript with inline marks, and a right pane that shows at most one amber whisper cue, an objection alert and eight rubric meters that stay 'provisional' until two turns of evidence exist. Debriefs are a split view with a sticky transcript and a provenance chip saying whether a model or the heuristic graded the call. The wizard is a full-screen dialog (Source, Persona, Scenario and rubric, Test call). The manager view reuses the rep components. The stack is shadcn on Radix, Tailwind 3, Geist and Geist Mono, with a custom SVG presence ring replacing the three.js orb.
presentations.strongest: Execution discipline and honesty. The palette is clean and well reasoned: near-black surfaces, one accent, and a note that the old #1D4ED8 blue is too dark on black. The live/dense split is a real design decision, not decoration. Replacing the react-three-fiber orb with a lightweight SVG presence ring removes the blurry orb the brief hates and cuts WebGL weight. The mobile-live section calls out two flaws I can see in the actual mobile-04 screenshot: the Next.js dev overlay covering the timer, and the red End button competing with send. The 'live meters and final score use one grader, so they agree by construction' rule is sound. It is a proposal a contributor can read and build.
presentations.weakest: It is the least distinctive. Dark, hairline-bordered, Cmd-K-first, Geist-typeset is the default look of developer tools in 2026, so a first screenshot will read as a competent Linear clone, not a sales-training product, and the proposal scores its own uniqueness a modest 7. Keyboard-first density suits power users, but the core user is a rep mid-call, and dense tables are a poor fit for non-technical managers and phone users. Dark-first conflicts with its own note that reps practise in bright offices. The stack claim that shadcn runs on Tailwind 3 and that staying there means 'no churn' is out of date. I attempted a Firecrawl lookup on shadcn and Tailwind v4 support but it was rate limited, so I rely on my own knowledge that shadcn has supported Tailwind v4 for some time. There is also an internal inconsistency: it says 'eight sales jobs' and then lists nine.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Slightly above baseline, quiet by design. A parallel coach stream emits typed events (cue, objection, step_done, rubric_delta), each with a confidence value and a transcript line reference. One cue at a time, only above a confidence threshold, auto-dismissed after 12 seconds unless pinned, with thumbs feedback logged. Target under 1.5 seconds with latency shown in the UI. Live meters read 'provisional' until two turns of evidence exist. The deductions: the proposal says the UI alone scores about 5 and the 6.0 depends on a coach stream that does not exist, and the single-cue rule makes coaching feel quiet rather than alive. It is safe and legible but not brilliant.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: At baseline, with no margin. It targets 120 persona-scenario pairs across 20-plus industries with a keyboard-row table, a 240px facet rail with counts, saved views and a preview drawer. It has compliance notes on regulated talk tracks (a good touch), one JSON file per persona validated by zod, and a wizard with source-cited drafts, auto-balancing weight sliders and a 60-second test call. But the proposal says the library only holds the bar at about 120 personas and falls below it under about 60, which means there is no headroom. The 'Edit on GitHub' and 'Propose persona PR' actions on each card are a good contributor on-ramp.

seat: Open-source maintainer and Codex fund reviewer

presentations.pitch: Switchboard Console turns the call into a dark phosphor-green console and keeps the reading screens (debrief, library, dashboard, print) on light paper. On a call you get a talk-track patch panel with six jacks that light as each step is hit, a real-audio oscilloscope in place of the blurry orb, a teleprinter transcript, and a Coach column with an amber whisper ticker above five rubric LEDs marked 'live estimate, unverified'. The best architectural idea is one shared evidence object: the live cue, the live LED and the final debrief quote are the same record, so coaching and grading cannot drift apart. The library is a faceted, cmdk-searchable board of 300+ JSON personas across 30+ jobs, with Built-in/Community/Mine badges. The wizard is a numbered 1-4 question flow that ends in a 2-minute test call and 'Export as PR'. For the fund, a 'Model switchboard' tray names the OpenAI model behind each job and shows live cost per call, and CI runs Codex review on persona-schema changes. It is built on shadcn/ui (Base UI), Tailwind v4 and IBM Plex. Fund-reviewer read: the terminal aesthetic suits a Codex-CLI audience and gives the README the most memorable hero GIF of the five. The cost is a vocabulary tax (Board, Patch, Ticket, Log), a 300-persona content promise and a two-theme QA load.
presentations.strongest: The OpenAI showcase is explicit and visible: a model tray with per-call cost, a README hero showing a real coach cue with the model named, 'Export as PR' for personas, and Codex review on schema changes. The shared evidence trail is also the most defensible coaching design in the batch. Naming models as plain facts, with no implied OpenAI endorsement, is the right posture for a fund application. The model name itself needs a fix: I confirmed gpt-realtime-1.5 exists (live since March 2026), but OpenAI's current Realtime guide uses gpt-realtime-2.1. Hard-coding 1.5 in the UI would date the app, so the label should read from config.
presentations.weakest: Three weaknesses. (1) Learnability: renaming the core areas Board, Patch, Call, Ticket and Log asks a new rep to learn a metaphor before practising, and the same goes for a sales manager evaluating it. (2) Content: 300 seeded personas is the largest promise in the set. A volunteer repo cannot review that many, and thin entries would make the library look padded to a reviewer who opens the folder. (3) Debrief honesty: it never addresses the visible defect in the current debrief screenshot, where the keyword fallback produces an F at 50% with an 'LLM grader failed' banner. A reviewer running the demo without an API key would hit exactly that path. Smaller points: one cue per 20 seconds can go silent in a fast objection exchange, and LED evidence on hover does not work on touch. 'Base UI is shadcn's default since July 2026' is unconfirmed (see lookups).
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Exceeds the baseline, roughly 6.3. A separate structured-output coach call returns one typed cue per rep turn (OBJECTION, NEXT QUESTION, TALK-TRACK STEP, TIME) with confidence and rubric ids. The talk-track jacks, rubric LEDs with evidence on hover, a Silent mode that keeps scoring, and one shared evidence trail cover every coaching element the brief names. Held back by the 20-second cooldown (few cues in a 3-minute call), the 2-second latency target that is stated but unmeasured, and no fallback when the coach call fails.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Exceeds the baseline, roughly 6.4. The library UI is the strongest of the five: faceted rail with live counts, cmdk search, difficulty LEDs, source badges, a dense table toggle, and one JSON file per persona so contributors add personas by PR. The wizard (source tray, numbered question cards, streaming build log, live persona card, rubric weights summing to 100, test call, Export as PR) is excellent. Held back by 300 personas being a content promise with no curation plan beyond a rubric test, and no mention of SSRF or PII handling for the product-URL and pasted-call inputs.

presentations.pitch: Clay Coach is a warm, tactile console built around one character: a soft-clay 3D caller bust (react-three-fiber, already a dependency) whose jaw follows the audio level and whose halo changes colour with state (sage when on track, amber when an objection lands, cobalt while the caller speaks). The 3D stays on the persona and the live caller only. Scorecards, dashboards and the team table stay flat with hairline rules. Light is the default, with first-class dark mode. The live call is a console: talk-track tracker and a 'next best question' card on the left, speaker-lane captions in the centre, and a right rail of five rubric bars that stay hatched while provisional and lock solid once a transcript quote confirms them, plus whisper cue cards and a Coach On/Quiet/Off switch. The debrief is a two-column scorecard with a medallion grade, a radar, a cue timeline showing which coaching was followed, and quotes that scrub audio to the exact second. The library is faceted with a 'New persona' first tile; each persona is a versioned JSON recipe including an avatar recipe, and the wizard tags every generated field with the source sentence it came from. A Model Ledger chip on each AI surface shows model, latency, tokens and cost per call. The stack is shadcn/ui on Base UI, Tailwind v4, Motion, Recharts and Bricolage Grotesque.
presentations.strongest: The Model Ledger is the best evidence-of-efficiency idea in the batch: model, latency, tokens and cost on every AI surface, plus a /contribute page with a Codex CLI quickstart, a good-first-issue board and a PR-review status tile. Its most fund-relevant move is linking the grader's reasoning to agreement with a human-scored golden set. Evals are what OpenAI-side reviewers trust, and no other proposal offers anything like it. Provenance chips on wizard fields (each generated trait jumps to its source sentence) are also a genuine credibility feature. It is honest about voice (ElevenLabs today, OpenAI Realtime as an option) and uses model names only, never the OpenAI logo.
presentations.weakest: The signature element, the 3D clay caller, is the one thing a sales-call console does not need, and it consumes the scarce maintainer capacity that should go into coaching and the library. It needs one WebGL canvas per screen, pre-rendered thumbnails, a static fallback, and a parametric avatar system (head shapes, palettes, accessories) that the phase plan never scopes. Contributors then have a second recipe surface to review. The library never states a persona count or names its job families, so it is the thinnest of the five on content. It also misses the visible 'F at 50% from keyword fallback' debrief defect. Playful clay will read as unserious to call-centre and enterprise buyers.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Roughly meets the baseline, 5.7. The design is good: typed cues each carrying a confidence value and the triggering transcript line, hatched-to-solid provisional rubric bars, a talk-track tracker, a Coach switch, and no final grade mid-call. But the 2-second cue budget rests on a fast parallel coach channel that is not designed in detail, and the stated fallback (post-turn hints) is a downgrade. No cooldown or rate rule is given, which risks cue spam.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Meets the baseline only, about 5.3. Facets (role, industry, difficulty, objection, mode, source), a versioned JSON recipe and a source-chip wizard with a 60-second test call are all sound. But there is no persona count and no list of sales jobs, the proposal itself calls breadth a content problem it does not solve, and the avatar recipe adds friction to every contribution. The UI is right in shape and unproven in content.

presentations.pitch: Call Record Console treats every object (Persona, Scenario, Call Record, Rubric, Member) as a CRM-style record page in an original dark console, with no Salesforce logo or blue chrome. All records share one header, tabs and a Path bar of talk-track stages (Open, Diagnose, Qualify, Handle objection, Close) that fills as the rep hits each stage, the same component before, during and after the call. The live call is three zones: a persona rail with buyer state and a mono timer, a transcript timeline where rubric hits pin as teal markers and coach lines sit inline in amber, and a utility panel with a whisper card, next-question chip, objection alert, Path tracker and a rubric meter whose bars link to evidence lines. The library is 120 personas across 24 jobs and 15 industries, with six facets, saved views (Ramp new hires, Pricing pushback), a sortable table and a six-tab persona record. The wizard takes a URL, job description, CRM export, ICP or pasted call, shows a source snippet on every field, ends in a 60-second dry run, and exports a PR-ready file. It keeps Tailwind 3 and uses shadcn on Radix, Geist and Tremor. Models are named where they act: a Coach chip on the console, a 'Graded by' footer on each debrief, and a per-session token and cost panel in Settings.
presentations.strongest: It is the most honest and maintainer-minded proposal. It catches the real defect in the current debrief (an F at 50% produced by the keyword fallback) and fixes it in scoring logic as well as UI, with an 'Estimate' chip instead of a letter grade. It refuses to claim OpenAI Realtime on the landing page until the adapter ships. It drops late coach cues rather than showing them stale. It keeps Tailwind 3, which means the lowest migration churn and the lowest chance of a half-finished rewrite. A persona JSON schema with a CI validator and a Codex CLI task to draft and validate persona files is a clean, believable contributor loop. The CRM-activity sync idea gives it the best sales-org story of the five.
presentations.weakest: Even without the logo, record pages, related lists and a Path bar read as CRM admin software, so its distinctiveness borrows the category rather than inventing one, and it invites trade-dress questions. Five objects and six persona tabs ask a rep to learn a sales-ops model before practising, and the 'three panels per screen' cap is a promise rather than a shown layout. The OpenAI showcase is the weakest of the five: the cost panel lives in Settings, not on the stage. Tremor's Tailwind 3 compatibility and a reported Vercel deal are unverified and every chart depends on it. Salesforce and HubSpot sync is planned scope that belongs after the core loop works. The 80-persona launch floor has no staffing plan.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Exceeds the baseline, about 6.0. A separate coach returns structured JSON (one-line cue, next best question, objection tag, rubric deltas), each tied to the justifying transcript line. Silent/Whisper/Full modes, a Path tracker, a rubric meter linked to evidence, a 'live estimate' label, and an honest Estimate chip when the heuristic grader runs. The 2.5-second drop rule is principled but means a slow coach silently produces nothing, and no measured latency is given. There is no cooldown rule.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Exceeds the baseline modestly, about 5.9. 120 personas over 24 jobs is a realistic and reviewable target, and the proposal honestly says to ship at least 80 before any public claim. Facets, saved views, table or card toggle, one JSON file per persona and a source-snippet wizard with dry run and PR export meet everything the brief asks. It lacks a wow factor and the content is still unstaffed.

presentations.pitch: Expressive Coaching Studio is a Material 3 Expressive redesign on MUI v7 in which each persona's temperament (friendly teal, skeptical amber, hostile red) seeds a full tonal palette via Google's Material Color Utilities, so the whole call screen re-tints as the buyer's mood shifts. It uses 28px corners, pill buttons, spring motion, Roboto Flex, Material Symbols, a morphing Start button and a shader orb driven by agent audio. The live call is three columns: orb with interest and trust meters, a transcript with coach markers, and a coach column where up to three cues stack and stay pinned until read, above seven rubric meters labelled provisional. The coach is a separate model channel; if it fails, a keyword checker keeps the talk track moving and a visible 'coaching paused' line appears. The debrief adds a live-versus-final score sparkline with markers where cues fired. The library is 120+ YAML persona packs, with URL-shareable filters and playlists. The wizard takes five input types, tags fields to source lines, runs a 60-second test drive with a 'Make harder' toggle, and can open a GitHub PR with the YAML pack. The fund angle is a model strip on the landing page and header with per-session cost, a seeded demo team and recorded sample call so reviewers can see coaching without API keys, and a planned 'Codex-reviewed' badge on accepted personas.
presentations.strongest: Two ideas are genuinely fund-friendly. First, the seeded demo team plus a recorded sample call, so a reviewer sees coaching and scoring without setting up keys. Second, graceful degradation on coach failure (a keyword fallback and a visible 'coaching paused' state), which is more robust than most of the batch. The live-versus-final sparkline is a smart way to show reps and reviewers how trustworthy the live estimates are. The wizard's 'open a GitHub PR with the YAML pack' is a direct contributor loop, and MUI is a library most contributors already know.
presentations.weakest: It is the largest and riskiest rewrite. It drops Tailwind and lucide, swaps in MUI, MUI X Data Grid, Recharts, three.js and Material Color Utilities, and gets only a custom approximation of Expressive, since MUI does not ship M3 Expressive shapes or springs (the proposal admits this). The Material look is itself recognisable as a template, which is the brief's diagnosis. Tinting a whole call screen, springing cues, morphing buttons and a shader orb all at once is a lot for a rep listening to a caller. The interest and trust meters and mood-driven tint need a mood signal the voice path does not produce today, a hidden dependency. Seven live meters do not match the editable five-criterion rubrics the app uses. A 'Codex-reviewed' badge for a workflow that is only planned, and a 'Powered by OpenAI' strip, both risk implying more than is true or endorsed. Temperament colour-coding invites stereotyping and contrast failures.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Roughly meets the baseline, 5.6. Typed cues linked to the triggering line, a pinned stack capped at three, Off/Subtle/Whisper levels, provisional meters and a failure fallback are all solid. But the simultaneous motion load (tint shifts, springs, orb, seven meters) works against a rep trying to listen, the 2-second target is aspirational, and the mood-driven meters lack a signal source.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Meets the baseline, about 5.7. 120+ YAML packs across the brief's job families, URL-shareable filters, playlists and a source-traced wizard with test drive and PR output cover the requirements. It is a content project larger than the UI work, and the proposal itself says it may launch smaller.

presentations.pitch: Copilot Rail Studio is a full-app redesign on shadcn/ui, Tailwind v4 tokens and Geist, with a light default and a dark stage for live calls. The centrepiece is a 360px copilot rail beside a speaker-labelled transcript. It holds a 'Live estimate' strip of five criterion bars with deltas, a talk-track stepper that ticks as steps are covered, and up to three typed cue cards (objection, next question, whisper, guardrail), each citing the turn and rubric criterion that triggered it. 'Use line' drops the suggested phrase into the composer without sending it, and the persona never sees cue text. The debrief has a sticky score ring, a grader-source chip (so a heuristic grade is labelled as such, with a re-grade action), evidence chips that highlight the exact transcript line, and 'Retry from turn 8', which branches practice from the missed objection. The library is 200+ JSON packs across about 18 job families with six live-count facets. The five-step wizard puts the generated JSON beside the form with a schema-valid badge, runs a dry-run chat, requires rubric weights to total 100, uses an allowlisted URL fetcher, and exports a pack PR. One Zod schema serves wizard, coach and grader. Each OpenAI job is named on screen (voice on the stage, coach in the rail footer, grader on the debrief, wizard on each persona), a Models page accepts any OpenAI-compatible base URL, and a Contributors page offers a copyable Codex CLI prompt.
presentations.strongest: It is the most fundable by a wide margin because it is the most executable and contributor-ready. One shared Zod schema across wizard, coach and grader is a maintainer-grade decision. The wizard's JSON preview shows contributors exactly which file a generated persona becomes. SSRF protection for the URL fetcher is designed in (the only proposal that does this). Its quality gates are measurable: p50 cue latency under about 2 seconds and cue precision on 30 scripted calls. It is also candid about scope: 'ship phases 1-3 for the fund application; the team view can slip' and 'claim Codex maintainer use only if true'. The grader-source chip honestly handles the keyword-fallback F visible in today's debrief screenshot. The Models page with any OpenAI-compatible base URL helps OSS credibility while still putting OpenAI models front and centre.
presentations.weakest: It is the least distinctive of the five. A dark side rail beside a transcript is the Gong/Balto pattern, it keeps today's blue (#1D4ED8) and ink (#071827), and it was designed from competitor write-ups because Mobbin returned no real live-coaching screens, so the visual claims are untested. The 'Phase 1 (S)' label for a Tailwind 3 to 4 migration, shadcn init, tokens and a mobile layout fix understates the work. A 360px rail squeezes the transcript at 1280px. 'Use line' makes sense in text mode but is unclear in voice mode, where the rep is speaking, not typing. Nine screens, a wizard and 200 seeded personas is a large load for a volunteer repo, and the 200 personas still need a review process.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Best of the five, roughly 6.9. A separate coach channel with a debounce, one cue per turn and an 8-second cooldown reads the last six turns, the rubric and talk-track state, and returns schema-checked cues that cite a turn and criterion. Live scores show partial credit, deltas and the quote that earned them, labelled 'Live estimate', and the final grade comes from a full-transcript pass with a visible fallback chip. Latency and precision have explicit acceptance gates. The only gap is voice-mode ergonomics of 'Use line'.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Exceeds the baseline, about 6.4. 200+ JSON packs (persona, talk track, objection bank and rubric together) across about 18 job families, a six-facet rail with counts, a CI schema check, a CONTRIBUTING rubric and a schema-valid wizard with a visible JSON panel and PR export. SSRF-aware context fetching is a plus. Content quality and review capacity, not UI, are the ceiling, as the proposal itself says.

presentations.pitch: Composed Coaching Console is a dark, calm coaching console on one fixed design system (shadcn, Tailwind v4, Geist, hairlines, teal for anything the AI wrote). The twist is that the AI picks which blocks appear for each call, from a closed set of typed blocks (ScoreHero, MomentReplay, CriterionCard, PatternCallout, DrillCTA, plus live cue blocks). It never writes markup, and every block must cite transcript turns that validate, with a classic fixed-order debrief as the fallback. On a live call the rep sees speaker lanes with a small score chip on each of their turns (+3 Discovery), a five-criterion rubric strip that ticks up as they cover ground, a next-best-question chip, talk-track dots, a coral objection bar, and at most two amber whisper cards that quote the exact line that triggered them and fade after 8 seconds. A Blind / Guided / Coached dial stays visible before, during and after the call. The debrief opens on the one turn that cost the deal, then criteria with playable quotes, patterns, and a drill for the weakest skill. The library is about 150 zod-validated persona packs. The wizard takes a job description, URL, CRM note or pasted call, fills a persona card field by field with a source chip on each field, lets the rep tune it by chat ('make them more skeptical'), runs a 60-second rehearsal, then saves or exports the same pack file a contributor would write. For the OpenAI fund it has the cleanest story: a model-slot strip on the landing page, grader model, rubric version and token cost in every debrief footer, a Realtime voice path next to ElevenLabs, and Codex reviewing persona PRs.
presentations.strongest: It is built around how coaches actually develop reps. It opens the debrief on the moment that cost the deal, not a letter grade. It puts a visible dial on how much scaffolding the rep gets (Blind, Guided, Coached), so coaching fades as skill grows. It quotes the trigger line in every cue, and the debrief ends in a drill on the weakest criterion. Every AI claim links to validated transcript turns, which reps and managers can trust. It also has the best fund story of the five: model, rubric version and cost are on screen, and the persona pack file is both the wizard's output and the contributor on-ramp.
presentations.weakest: The generative layout is the least valuable and riskiest part. Reps and managers want the same scorecard shape every time so they can compare calls, and the proposal's own fixed-order fallback admits the composition step can fail. The real coaching value (MomentReplay, DrillCTA, scaffold dial) does not need generative ordering, so I would ship those in a fixed order first and keep composition as an experiment. The D score depends on a sub-1.5-second coach stream that does not exist yet, and the three-cues-per-minute cap makes coaching sparse. Effort is labelled L but stacks a Tailwind v4 migration, AI SDK UI, AI Elements and a block registry, so it is really XL. The family list is only six (SDR cold, AE discovery, CS, support, collections, recruiting), with industry carrying the rest. The dark navy plus teal look is tasteful but close to generic dark-tech. Radix is still supported, but shadcn now defaults to Base UI (I confirmed the July 2026 changelog), so the stack should be pinned deliberately.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Exceeds baseline (6.9), conditional on latency. It has every baseline element (whisper cues, next-best question, objection alert, talk-track progress, live rubric). It adds per-turn score chips, cues that quote their trigger line, an Ask coach button and a three-position scaffolding dial. Live numbers are labelled estimates and the full-rubric grader stays canonical. It falls to baseline if cues land later than about 2 seconds, and the 3-cues-per-minute cap is a sensible guard against overload. This is the strongest live-coaching model of my five by a small margin over P02.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Slightly above baseline (6.4). About 150 packs across 18 industries, filterable by job family, industry, difficulty, objection type and mode, with personal-best rings and a dashed Build your own tile first. The wizard is among the best: a chat-plus-card draft with a source chip per field, tune presets, a 60-second rehearsal and a PR-ready export. Six job families is narrower than the brief's list, and 150 reviewed personas are a content project the UI cannot solve.

presentations.pitch: Live Desk Cockpit is the safe, shippable one. It takes the Catalyst-style app shell (persistent left sidebar with Practice, Library, Progress, Team and Settings, a Cmd-K palette, a four-tab mobile bar) and rebuilds it from MIT parts (shadcn/ui, cmdk, Motion, Recharts), because Catalyst's own code is under the restricted Tailwind Plus licence and cannot go in an MIT repo (my lookup supports this). Library, pre-call, debrief, progress and team pages are light. The live call switches to a dark three-zone cockpit: persona and talk-track ticks on the left, a presence ring and transcript with objection chips in the centre, and a right coach rail with up to three cue cards (whisper, objection alert with a suggested reply), per-criterion meters (not started, partial, covered) and a pace gauge. A criterion only turns covered when a transcript quote backs it, and when the grader is down the rail shows a grey Heuristic badge, not a fake number. The debrief has a moment timeline and a Replay this moment button that drops the rep back at the turn they fumbled, with the same persona state. The library is job-family shelves with a faceted filter rail and CI-checked badges (120 personas, 60 scenarios). The wizard is a prompt box with source chips, clarifying questions the AI asks the rep, a live preview with provenance chips, and a test call. For the fund: a models chip row in the cockpit, a Settings > Models page with each model's job and per-call cost, Realtime selectable beside ElevenLabs, and a Codex PR-review workflow that checks schema and rubric weights.
presentations.strongest: Replay this moment is the best deliberate-practice idea in my set, because it lets the rep redo the exact turn they fumbled instead of the whole call. The trust rules are also excellent for enablement: a criterion is covered only with a quote behind it, cues never reach the persona or audio channel, and the app shows an honest Heuristic badge rather than a stale score. The clarifying-question step in the wizard asks the rep to fill gaps rather than letting the model invent details. It has the most enterprise-ready information architecture (settings for rubrics, models and cost, security; roster; assign with due date; consent banner), and it is the most incremental migration, staying on Tailwind 3 with routes preserved.
presentations.weakest: It is the least distinctive design in the set. A sidebar, white cards and a blue primary is close to the default SaaS template the brief criticises, and the dark cockpit panel is doing all the work on identity. Dark cockpit plus light pages doubles QA and needs AA checks on amber and teal text. It has no visible coaching-intensity dial, so there is no way to fade scaffolding as a rep improves. Three stacked cue cards plus meters plus a pace gauge risk overload. The wizard has eight steps, which is long. The D (5.6) and E (5.3) self-scores are explicitly conditional on per-turn scoring shipping and on 100 reviewed personas. On mobile the End button sits inside a sheet behind a confirm, which is safe against mis-taps but slow in a real emergency. The Codex 'Build a persona' page and PR workflow are still plans.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Meets and just exceeds baseline (6.0). It covers whisper, objection alert with a suggested reply, talk-track ticks and a pace (talk ratio) gauge, and it has the best honesty rules on scoring. It loses ground because there is no coach-level control, the three-card stack could overload a rep mid-sentence, and the debounced per-turn call has no stated latency budget. It is a competent, standard cockpit, not a breakthrough.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: At baseline plus a little (6.0). Thirteen job-family shelves, seven facets with counts (role, industry, difficulty, objection, channel, length), a CI-checked badge and duplicate-to-edit give broad coverage and a clean contributor path. The wizard's clarifying questions and rubric-sums-to-100 check are good. It only reaches this score if about 100 reviewed personas ship. The 120 personas plus 60 scenarios are fewer than P02 or P22, and the eight-step wizard is heavy.

presentations.pitch: Geist Signal Console is a monochrome, dev-tool-grade console for sales reps. It uses Geist Sans and Mono at three weights, 1px hairline borders, black primary buttons and shadcn/ui on Radix, with dark mode designed first. Exactly one colour is allowed to mean something: a teal signal that lights only when the AI coach has something to say, as a 1px ring that pulses while a cue is live. The live call is three resizable panes: a call pane (state pill, mono timer, mic meter, End and grade behind a confirm), a hairline transcript with inline markers like 'Objection: price', and a coach rail with a Next move card, a 'Why? line 6' evidence link, Accept / Dismiss / Not helpful, six rubric meters that tick with mono deltas, and talk-track progress. It states hard budgets: first cue within 2 seconds at p50, meters within 4 seconds, one cue per turn, with a Silent / Whisper / Guided level. The library is 200 persona-and-scenario pairs in 20 industry packs, each persona a versioned JSON file with a licence field, shown in a Sheet with Fork and View file on GitHub. The wizard lists what it found in your source (with quote chips and include checkboxes) before drafting any field, marks every generated field as quoted or inferred in amber, runs a dry run, then saves or exports a PR. The same zod schema doubles as the OpenAI Structured Outputs schema. For the fund: a provenance chip with model and latency on every AI output, cost per session on the dashboard, and an honest line that Realtime voice is planned, not claimed.
presentations.strongest: It has the best-engineered coaching loop and the best wizard grounding. Coach cues have explicit latency and frequency budgets, an evidence link, and Not helpful feedback that becomes a contributor eval set, so coach quality can improve in the open. The wizard's 'what I found' step with quote chips and amber 'inferred' marking attacks the biggest risk in AI persona generation, which is hallucinated buyer details. One zod schema serves the persona file, CI and OpenAI Structured Outputs. It is also unusually honest for a fund application: it does not claim Realtime voice until it ships, and it names cost per session. I verified that Geist is licensed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 (and is on Google Fonts), so the licence worry listed in the proposal is a non-issue for an MIT repo.
presentations.weakest: It looks like Vercel with a teal dot. The proposal itself warns that monochrome reads cold to a sales audience, and a fund reviewer may remember nothing about the look. For reps that coldness matters: sales people respond to energy and feedback, not an IDE feel. Accept, Dismiss and Not helpful on every cue add interaction burden in the middle of a live call. The 2-second p50 budget roughly doubles per-turn API cost, and the only answer is a per-session cap. Two hundred reviewed persona pairs are a human-content bottleneck with no named owner, and the proposal pasted a Mobbin usage notice into its risks list, which is noise. Keeping Tailwind 3 defers a second migration to a later PR. SaaS viability is the weakest here because a developer-console aesthetic does not suit sales ops buyers.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Exceeds baseline (6.8). It has one cue per turn with a visible reason, a 'Coach, private' label so cues never read as caller speech, Silent / Whisper / Guided levels, live meters with deltas, objection markers inline in the transcript, and an opt-in whispered TTS cue for voice mode. Stated latency budgets and a feedback loop make it the most measurable coaching design of the five. Mid-call Accept/Dismiss/Not helpful is a small usability tax.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Clearly above baseline (6.8), the best of my five. Two hundred pairs in 20 industry packs filtered by exactly the brief's facets (role, industry, difficulty, objection), curated rows, a table toggle, last-score on each card, Fork and View file on GitHub, and a versioned licence field. The wizard (find, then draft, then dry run, then export PR) is the most grounded. The 200-pair target is a content job with no seeding plan, and it falls below 5 if only a few dozen ship.

presentations.pitch: Editorial Ledger is a Swiss-grid, paper-and-ink application: a 12-column grid, hairline rules instead of cards and shadows, Newsreader serif for titles, Inter for UI and JetBrains Mono for every score and timer. Primary buttons are ink, and one vermilion colour is reserved for coach cues, objection alerts and End and grade. The live call is the only night-theme screen, so 'live' reads through a state change. Its signature idea is margin cues: each coaching note is pinned beside the transcript line that triggered it, so the rep sees why it appeared. A talk-track ledger ticks down the left, a rubric panel on the right shows six criteria as thin bars with provisional 'est.' numbers, and next-best-question chips sit above the composer. Coaching intensity (Silent, Cues, Cues and live score) is chosen before the call. The debrief reads like a printed report: a 120px serif score, 'Evidence: 9 of 9 claims quoted', numbered strengths and gaps linked to transcript lines, a criteria ledger with a 1-to-5 scale and verbatim quotes, and a note on which live numbers changed when the grader replaced them. The library is a facet rail (role, industry, difficulty, objection, source: built-in or community) with counts and URL-shareable filters, plus a preview drawer showing the buyer brief and rubric weights before the rep starts. The four-step wizard cites the source snippet for each generated field, requires rubric weights to total 100, runs a dry run and exports a PR. The colophon names the OpenAI models on every screen, with AGENTS.md and Codex reviewing persona PRs. I confirmed the Base UI default claim: shadcn's own July 2026 changelog says new projects default to Base UI.
presentations.strongest: It is the most evidence-first and the most honest. Margin cues show exactly why a cue fired. Live scores are marked estimates, and the debrief lists which numbers changed after the grader ran, which builds rep trust. The report-style debrief is the most readable of the five, and the 1-to-5 segmented scale per criterion matches how managers already score calls. The library is the most honest about quality: ship 60 polished personas first and label the rest 'community drafts', with a Source facet to tell them apart. Showing rubric weights before the call is real enablement practice. The look is the most distinctive and premium of the set, and the colophon makes OpenAI usage visible without shouting.
presentations.weakest: Austerity is the risk. A paper-and-serif skin can read as a publication or a docs site, not the cutting-edge AI voice product the brief asks for, and the only looping motion is a waveform strip, so the live call can feel like a text transcript with annotations. The coach has no hard latency promise: if cues miss about 2 seconds they become post-turn, which the proposal itself says drops D to baseline. It claims 200 personas across 20 sales jobs but names only 15. F1 is self-scored 4 and the proposal admits differentiation rests on self-hosting and bring-your-own-key, not design. Three font families and a lazy-loaded 3D orb add weight. Base UI is young and may need a React Aria fallback for complex comboboxes.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Slightly above baseline (6.2). The margin-pinned cue is the best explanation mechanism in the set, and the 'est.' to evidence handoff is excellent. It has next-best-question chips, objection alerts, talk-track ticks and a pre-call intensity choice. At most one cue per turn is disciplined. It loses points because the 1.5-second target has a post-turn fallback, margin cues scroll with the transcript, and the call screen is text-heavy for a voice product.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Slightly above baseline (6.3). Faceted rail with counts, URL-shareable filters, built-in versus community tiers, a preview drawer with buyer brief and rubric weights, and Fork. The four-step wizard cites its sources and enforces weights summing to 100. It is honest that content is the bottleneck, but the seed set is 60 polished personas, so it meets the standard only after the community fills the rest.

presentations.pitch: Keynote Bento is the most polished-looking of the five: a light bento grid for everything reviewed (landing, library, pre-call, debrief, progress, team) and one fixed dark stage for the live call and the landing hero. White hairline tiles with 28px radii sit on a #F5F5F7 canvas, with Geist display type at keynote scale, spring motion that reflows tiles, and shadcn/ui on Base UI with Tailwind v4. The live call is split 62/38. The left stage has an orb whose ring shows listening, thinking or speaking without relying on colour, a rep-versus-caller talk-time meter and two big caption lines. The right rail is a bento of a six-second whisper tile, a next-question tile, an objection alert that appears only when triggered, six-step talk-track progress, and a live rubric with delta chips (+4, -2) that tap through to the evidence quote. Coach levels are Off, Whisper and Full. The debrief has a grade hero, a score timeline that marks where a cue changed the call, criterion tiles with evidence chips that jump to the transcript, and a Practice next tile. The library is the broadest on paper: 150 personas across 25 job families, a natural-language 'Describe a buyer' search, facets for rep job, buyer role, industry, difficulty and objection type, a voice sample in the preview drawer, and a Build with AI tile first. The wizard streams a persona card field by field, with weight sliders that sum to 100 and a 60-second dry run, then exports as a contribution. The OpenAI story is visible: model chips on every AI surface, grader and token cost on each debrief, Realtime as a first-class voice choice, and a Built with Codex contributing guide.
presentations.strongest: The mobile and visual polish is the best of the five, and it fixes the current app's worst problems directly: the cramped mobile header, the red End button competing with the composer, and a live score pill above the fold. Its live rail is the most checklist-complete (whisper, next question, objection alert, talk track, live rubric deltas tied to quotes) and it adds a talk-time meter, a real sales-coaching metric. Separating 'rep job' from 'buyer role' in the library is a smart enablement distinction. 25 job families and voice previews give the best 'every sales job' feel. The score timeline showing where a cue changed the call gives a rep a concrete before-and-after.
presentations.weakest: Bento is now a common template, so the look is polished but not distinctive, and the glowing orb on a dark stage can read as a gimmick if accents are overused. Five live tiles plus captions risk overload, and only two caption lines means the rep cannot scan back through the conversation. The wizard is the least grounded of the five: it streams a persona card but does not say that each field cites its source. The 2-second cue budget is unproven (the proposal itself says it only exceeds baseline if latency holds under 2 seconds). It stacks a Tailwind 3 to 4 rewrite of every class on top of a Base UI switch. I confirmed shadcn made Base UI the default in July 2026, so the stack choice is sound, but the proposal's own sources disagree on Radix maintenance. The 150-persona seed is a content job, and the proposal says E falls to about 4.6 without it. Realtime voice adds per-minute cost.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Baseline plus (6.1). It has every standard element plus a talk-time meter and evidence-linked rubric deltas, with a clean mobile treatment. Coach levels (Off, Whisper, Full) exist. Cues fade at six seconds and never cover captions. It does not stand out on coaching quality or measurability: no feedback loop, no stated budget beyond 2 seconds, and a busy tile rail.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Slightly above baseline (6.4). The broadest family coverage (150 personas, 25 families), five facets, natural-language search, voice-sample preview, contributor credit on tiles, and a Build with AI entry point. The wizard is a competent four-step flow but lacks per-field provenance. It meets the standard only if the 150 seed personas actually ship.

presentations.pitch: Live Ledger turns every persona, scenario, rubric and talk track into an editable document, puts the library, wizard, debrief and progress screens on a warm paper canvas, and flips to an always-dark three-column cockpit for the call itself. During a call a separate coach model reads each finished turn and returns one whisper cue (at most one per 20 seconds, objections jump the queue), a talk-track step and rubric evidence. Five meters labelled 'live estimate' flash a teal delta when evidence lands, and each cue has a Why link to the rubric line it serves. The final grade re-runs the same rubric over the full transcript, so live and debrief agree, and a fallback score shows as an amber 'Estimate only' instead of today's red F. The library targets 120+ personas across 12 job families. A five-input wizard (job description, product URL, CRM notes, ICP, pasted call) streams a draft into a live document, forces rubric weights to total 100, redacts PII by default and ends in a two-minute test call. A manager view adds a team heatmap, a coaching queue and a rep drawer with supervisor notes. A Model passport in Settings shows which OpenAI model does each job and what each call costs. My lens: this is the product a training company or sales-enablement team would actually license, but it is also the heaviest build in my set.
presentations.strongest: Best enterprise story of the five. PII redaction on by default for pasted transcripts is the first thing a call-center security review asks about, and no other proposal has it. Editable persona, rubric and script documents let a customer own its content, which is what training companies pay to keep. The manager view (heatmap, coaching queue, supervisor notes as doc blocks) and the Model passport with per-call cost give a buyer both control and cost visibility. Labelling estimates honestly fixes a real trust bug I can see in the current debrief screenshot, where a keyword fallback shows a red F as if it were a grade. The 'Replay moment' that shows the cue which should have fired doubles as a coaching-quality check.
presentations.weakest: Scope, plus a hole in the open-source pitch. The TipTap block editor is a multi-week sink the proposal itself admits, and 'several months for one developer' for XL is optimistic. It never says what format personas take in the repo. If they are TipTap JSON, pull-request diffs are unreadable, which undercuts the 'reviewable persona file' and Codex persona-review story the fund pitch rests on. The fix is Markdown or YAML files with the editor rendering from them. The Notion-style document metaphor also adds a click between a rep and 'Start call' and can read as a productivity tool rather than a sales trainer. The F scores (6/6/3) are asserted, not argued. I checked the repo: it has no AGENTS.md, no .github folder and no Codex mention, so the Codex-assisted PR review is entirely future work.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Exceeds the standard modestly (about 6.3). Separate coach model with structured outputs so the persona never breaks character, rate-limited cues with objection priority, talk-track step tracking, five live rubric meters with evidence deltas, inline coach notes on rep turns, a talk-ratio meter, a Why link to the rubric line, and a full re-grade at the end so numbers never contradict. Not yet proven: the 2-second cue target has no measurement harness, a second model call per turn adds cost, and there is no labelled eval set to show cues help.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Exceeds the open-source standard (about 6.4) on design. 120+ personas, at least eight per family, filters for job, industry, difficulty, objection type and mode, a five-input wizard with streaming preview, weights validated to 100, PII redaction and a test call. Gaps: 120 is a content target, not shipped content; the family list mixes jobs and industries and omits real estate, which the brief names; and the repo file format is unspecified.

presentations.pitch: Practice Graph Studio makes the project look and behave like a repository a maintainer would be proud of, while keeping the call itself calm and sales-native. The header has a repo-style wordmark, MIT badge and star link. Every persona is a versioned, schema-checked file with a Source tab and an Edit-as-PR action. The wizard is a chat on the left and a live persona card on the right, where every generated field shows the source sentence it came from, then a 60-second test call, then a file diff. The live cockpit has a rubric rail whose bars stay dotted until the grader confirms them, six talk-track steps, and one cue at a time that auto-dismisses after 8 seconds with a 'why' link to the exact transcript line. Reps choose a coaching level (Silent, Cues, Full), which directly answers the risk that whispers make reps stop listening. Progress is a 52-week practice graph shaded by score band, not volume, so a streak means improvement. The manager view has a roster with mini graphs, a 'Needs you' queue with Assign drill, and an objection-coverage heatmap. The business model is stated plainly: MIT core free, paid hosted team analytics and manager queue, licensing to call centers and training firms.
presentations.strongest: The clearest path from open source to revenue in the set, at L effort rather than XL. The free core is the library, wizard and live coach; the paid layer is the manager queue and hosted analytics, which is what a sales-ops buyer would pay for. The practice graph is a genuine retention loop (habit plus quality guard) for self-serve SaaS. Personas as schema-checked files with community-source labels and a PR flow is the cleanest contributor funnel and the most credible place for Codex to do real work, namely reviewing persona PRs for schema, bias and safety. Provenance chips on each wizard field and coaching levels are trust features no one else has. It stays on shadcn and Tailwind, the stack contributors and coding agents already know. Cost and latency in the call footer show OpenAI usage honestly.
presentations.weakest: It looks like a developer tool, and the buyers I would sell to are sales managers. Repo header, monospace everywhere, commit-log session lists and path-style breadcrumbs risk reading as GitHub cosplay, and the proposal's own risk list concedes it. Launch library is only 60 personas, the smallest in the set, against a brief that asks for a large library. Persona-by-PR assumes GitHub literacy most reps lack, so a non-PR 'submit' path is needed. One grader streams both cues and scores and the debrief reuses its output, so the final grade may not be a full-transcript re-run, and the proposal never states that the persona stays blind to coaching. Both need to be written down. Codex PR review is a planned action only: I checked the repo and it has no AGENTS.md, no .github folder and no Codex references today.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Exceeds the standard slightly (about 6.0). Per-turn streamed grader with a 1.5 second target, Silent/Cues/Full levels, one auto-dismissing cue, a 'why' link to the exact quote, dotted-until-confirmed rubric bars, talk-track ticking, objection alerts, suggested bridge in text mode, and latency plus cost in the footer. Weak spots: no explicit rate limit beyond one at a time, a single grader doing both jobs creates a latency single point of failure (it does specify a fall-back to post-turn scoring), and live cue quality has no eval plan.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Meets the standard, just above (about 5.4). The mechanics are the best in the set (files, CI schema check, official vs community source, counts on filters, Good first persona label, provenance-chip wizard, test call, diff and PR), but 60 personas at launch across 13 job types is about four or five per job, which is thin for a library meant to cover every sales role. Fix by gating launch on 120+ or by seeding through the wizard itself.

presentations.pitch: Patch Bay Console turns the live call into a physical instrument. A coach-intensity knob (Off, Hints, Full) sets how often the coach speaks. Six talk-track step keys latch when the grader marks a step covered. A rubric rack of five channel strips shows covered, partial or missed LEDs that move after each rep turn, a 12-LED ring shows voice level, and a cue strip uses green, amber and red LEDs with a Coach me key. Everything outside the call uses the same tokens on a calm bone-colored paper surface. A separate coach call keeps the persona in character, and a model ledger on every debrief shows the grader model, tokens and estimated cost. The library targets about 240 personas but ships 60 reviewed ones first, and the four-step wizard (Source, Persona, Rubric, Dry run) drafts persona and rubric weights from a URL, job description, CRM notes or a pasted call. It is the most original idea in the set and the only one built around a control the rep operates rather than a panel the rep reads.
presentations.strongest: The most memorable demo in the pool, and the coach-intensity knob is a real product idea worth stealing in plain form: letting a rep dial help up or down is the direct answer to cue fatigue. Self-scoring is honest (D 5.3, E 5.2), the model ledger is a good transparency touch, and the phased plan keeps a working demo live throughout. Status is always colour plus glyph plus text, which is good accessibility practice.
presentations.weakest: As a business bet it is the weakest of my five. Hardware skeuomorphism is a novelty that enterprise buyers and reps taking thirty calls a day may read as a toy, and the proposal concedes it. It requires a custom SVG instrument kit (knob, LED ring, channel strip, step key) with hand-built keyboard and screen-reader support that a small open-source team must maintain forever. Cues stay off by default until a labelled eval set exists, so day-one coaching is at baseline. The look is two systems stitched together. Worst for fund credibility: it states that Codex already does PR review and release notes in this repo. I checked, and there is no AGENTS.md, no .github folder and no Codex mention in the README or CONTRIBUTING. An OpenAI reviewer would check that first. The manager view admits real-call coaching is not built (a greyed slot).
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: At the standard (about 5.4). Incremental grader per turn, separate coach call, on-demand Coach me key, intensity knob, step keys and per-criterion LEDs with evidence tooltips. That is a complete loop. But cues are not on by default, the 2.5 second target is the slowest stated, there is no rate limit besides the knob, and quality depends on an eval set that does not exist.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Right at the baseline (about 5.0). The wizard is solid (three entry modes, field-level regenerate, weight knobs summing to 100, dry run, Contribute exports persona JSON) and the filters are complete, but launch is 60 reviewed personas against a 240 target, the proposal calls the content work a risk, and provenance of generated fields is thin ('drafted from 3 sources').

presentations.pitch: Signal Desk is a dark-first, source-owned design system (Ark UI behavior, Panda CSS tokens, Park UI-style components copied into the repo) that turns the trainer into a coaching cockpit. A right-hand coach rail shows one amber whisper card at a time (at most one per 20 seconds, with the verbatim trigger quote and a Why link), a talk-track stepper, a next-best question and five rubric meters that show tracking ranges rather than grades. The final grade re-runs the full evidence grader so the debrief never contradicts the live view, and the debrief opens with one Instrument Serif verdict line, a score ring, a radar against the last attempt and a 'Heuristic estimate' badge on fallback. The library seeds 150+ reviewed personas on a clear taxonomy, and a five-step wizard drafts persona, scenario and rubric with a provenance chip on every field ('from product page, para 2'), requires weights to total 100, runs a 60-second dry run and saves nothing until the rep approves. Model chips on every stage show model ID, latency and cost, OpenAI Realtime is a first-class voice engine, and a human-labelled gold-debrief eval lives in the repo behind a Trust panel.
presentations.strongest: The best answer to the question every enterprise buyer asks first: can I trust the AI score? It is the only proposal that commits to a measured answer, a human-labelled grader eval in the repo with a visible Trust panel. That is also exactly the kind of artifact OpenAI reviewers respect. Model chips with latency and cost per stage make OpenAI usage auditable, and Realtime as a first-class voice option addresses the fact that voice is ElevenLabs-only today (I confirmed this in the README). Provenance on every wizard field, 'tracking ranges not grades' wording and AGENTS.md plus a Codex PR review workflow in the plan give it the most complete Codex story. The look is polished and editorial without the gimmick risk.
presentations.weakest: The stack is a velocity and contributor tax. Panda CSS, Ark and Park have far smaller ecosystems than Tailwind and shadcn, so fewer contributors and fewer ready-made patterns for coding agents. It removes Tailwind entirely, rewriting every component, and the proposal itself says two styling systems must not coexist for long. That is the heaviest migration in my set, with XL effort. D and E (self-scored 5.3 and 5.4) are conditional on a coach channel and 150 reviewed personas that do not exist yet. Dark with teal and amber is now the default AI-product skin, and the proposal flags the risk of a generic look. As of today the repo has no AGENTS.md or .github folder, so the Codex workflow is all future work.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Exceeds the standard slightly (about 6.1). Coach model on every finished turn using the last six turns, rubric and step, returning one cue (max one per 20 seconds), an objection tag, step progress and rubric deltas each tied to a verbatim quote, a next-best question, 2-second target with fallback to after-turn cues, and a full re-grade at the end. Missing: a quiet mode on the screens, and cost is multiplied per turn, which the proposal admits.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Exceeds the standard slightly (about 6.3) on design. 150+ reviewed versioned persona files, a defined taxonomy (role, industry, difficulty, objection type), faceted rail with removable chips, and the strongest wizard trust model (provenance chips, weights total 100, dry run, nothing saves until approved). The count is a content target and the wizard has no PII redaction mentioned.

presentations.pitch: Swipe-to-Rehearse Coach Studio is a practical, dark-first call cockpit on a light library, built on shadcn/ui, Tailwind v4 and Geist, with swipe demoted to an opt-in 90-second objection-drill deck. The live call has a left talk-track rail, a timestamped transcript and a right coach panel with live rubric meters and delta chips labelled 'live estimate', one whisper card about two seconds after the rep's turn, an Ask the coach box, a talk-to-listen meter and a cost-per-call ticker. The coach is a separate stream so the persona never sees coaching, with a quiet mode and a rule that scoring lags rather than blocks the call. Violet is reserved for anything an AI wrote. The debrief has a call timeline with colored criterion markers that jump to transcript lines and a 'Biggest miss' card that plays the better line in the AI voice. The library is a filterable grid of 150+ personas across 20+ jobs, stored as plain JSON files with a CI validator, and the four-step wizard accepts any source, takes edit requests in a side chat, shows a cost estimate before generating and exports the same file format for contributions. On mobile the coach is a bottom sheet with peek, half and full snap points.
presentations.strongest: The most shippable plan and the most complete library design. It uses the stack contributors already know, plain JSON persona files with a CI validator (easy PRs, easy Codex review), a wizard with chat-style refinement and a cost estimate before generation (a good enterprise cost-control touch), 150+ personas across 20+ jobs, and a Playwright screenshot baseline across nine screens, two themes and two widths. Mobile is the most thought through: sheet snap points, wake lock, haptic tick, long-press to end. The 'Biggest miss' card playing the better line in an AI voice is a strong OpenAI voice showcase. Micro-drills of 90 seconds are a real mobile habit loop for self-serve SaaS.
presentations.weakest: It is the least distinctive design, and the idea in its name is the riskiest. Shadcn plus Geist plus a violet accent is the default modern SaaS template the brief calls out as the problem, and a swipe deck reads as a dating app to enterprise buyers, which its own risk list concedes. Nothing here gives a reviewer or a customer a reason to remember it over Second Nature or Yoodli. The proposal gives no self-scores and no business case, so F1 to F3 are never argued. Cues are not tied to a quoted transcript line, so a rep cannot check why one fired. Codex use is a documented intention only: the repo has no AGENTS.md, no .github folder and no Codex mention today. Peers advanced it 3/5, the weakest vote in my set.
presentations.live_coaching_verdict: Slightly above the standard (about 5.8). Separate coach stream, whisper card within about two seconds, delta chips marked live estimate, objection banner, Ask the coach, talk-listen meter, quiet mode, heavier-model final grade, lagging-not-blocking behavior. Weaker than P09, P17 and P44 on evidence: cues do not cite the quote they rest on and there is no eval plan.
presentations.persona_library_verdict: Exceeds the standard slightly (about 6.0). 150+ personas as plain JSON across 20+ jobs, a CI validator, filters for job, industry, difficulty, objection and mode, saved filter sets, My library vs Built-in vs Community, and a four-step wizard with chat edits, cost estimate, provenance badge, dry run and exportable file. No PII redaction for pasted calls and CRM notes, and the count is a content target.
